chapters.title: The reader and his two transmitters
paragraphs: Ibn ʿĀmir: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir al-Yaḥṣabī, the reader of Shām (Damascus) and the fourth of the ten readers. He was born in 21 AH and died in 118 AH. He learned the Quran from the Companion Abū al-Dardāʾ and from al-Mughīrah ibn Abī Shihāb, and has the shortest chain to the Prophet among the seven readers.
Hishām: Hishām ibn ʿAmmār al-Dimashqī (153–245 AH), the first transmitter, who received the reading through Ibn ʿĀmir's students.
Ibn Dhakwān: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Aḥmad ibn Dhakwān (173–242 AH), the second transmitter, imam of the Umayyad Mosque in his time.

Way of transmission: Everything here follows the Shāṭibiyyah of Imam al-Shāṭibī and is described by comparison with Ḥafṣ. Where no transmitter is named, the rule belongs to both Hishām and Ibn Dhakwān.

chapters.title: The basmalah between two surahs
paragraphs: Beginning a surah: Like every reader, Ibn ʿĀmir says the basmalah when beginning any surah except al-Tawbah, and between al-Nās and al-Fātiḥah.

Between two surahs: He has three ways of joining the end of one surah to the next: with the basmalah, with sakt (a short pause without breath) and no basmalah, or with waṣl (joining directly) and no basmalah. Ḥafṣ has only the basmalah.

With the basmalah: One may stop on both sides of it, join on both sides, or stop after the surah and join the basmalah to the next one. Joining it to the end of the surah and then stopping is not allowed.

The four Zuhr surahs: These are al-Qiyāmah, al-Muṭaffifīn, al-Balad and al-Humazah. Before them some scholars chose sakt for one who otherwise joins by waṣl, and the basmalah for one who otherwise uses sakt.
Al-Anfāl to al-Tawbah: There is no basmalah. As for all readers, one may stop, make sakt, or join directly.

chapters.title: Sūrat al-Fātiḥah
paragraphs: The word maliki: Ibn ʿĀmir reads مَلِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ (1:4) without an alif after the mīm. Ḥafṣ reads مَالِكِ.
Verse count: Unlike Ḥafṣ, Ibn ʿĀmir does not count the basmalah as a verse of al-Fātiḥah; صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ is the sixth verse and the rest is the seventh.

chapters.title: Hāʾ al-kināyah (the pronoun hāʾ)
paragraphs: General rule: Between two vowelled letters the pronoun hāʾ is lengthened with ṣilah of two ḥarakāt, or four when a hamzah follows, as in مَالَهُ أَخْلَدَهُ.
The word arjiʾhu: In 7:111 and 26:36 Ibn ʿĀmir adds a sākin hamzah. Hishām reads أَرْجِئْهُ with ḍammah and ṣilah; Ibn Dhakwān reads أَرْجِئْهِ with kasrah and no ṣilah. Ḥafṣ reads أَرْجِهْ.

Six words with kasrah: Ibn ʿĀmir reads the hāʾ with kasrah and ṣilah in يُؤَدِّهِ إِلَيْكَ (3:75, twice), نُؤْتِهِ مِنْهَا (3:145 twice, 42:20), نُوَلِّهِ مَا تَوَلَّىٰ وَنُصْلِهِ جَهَنَّمَ (4:115), فَأَلْقِهِ إِلَيْهِمْ (27:28) and وَيَتَّقِهِ (24:52). Hishām has a second way: kasrah without ṣilah. Ḥafṣ differs in وَيَتَّقْهِ, where he alone makes the qāf sākin, and in فَأَلْقِهْ.

Three words without ḍammah or ṣilah: Ibn ʿĀmir reads أَنسَانِيهِ (18:63) and عَلَيْهِ اللَّهَ (48:10) with kasrah on the hāʾ, and in the second the lām of the name Allāh is thin; Ḥafṣ reads both with ḍammah. In فِيهِ مُهَانًا (25:69) Ibn ʿĀmir reads the kasrah short, while Ḥafṣ lengthens it with ṣilah.
The word yarḍahu: In يَرْضَهُ لَكُمْ (39:7) Hishām has two ways: a short ḍammah like Ḥafṣ (preferred), or sukūn, يَرْضَهْ. Ibn Dhakwān reads the ḍammah with ṣilah.
The word yarahu: In خَيْرًا يَرَهُ and شَرًّا يَرَهُ (99:7–8) Hishām reads the hāʾ sākin, يَرَهْ, in both verses.

chapters.title: Madd and qaṣr
paragraphs: Madd muttaṣil and munfaṣil: Ibn ʿĀmir lengthens both to four ḥarakāt (tawassuṭ), like Ḥafṣ. Examples: السَّمَاءِ and جَاءَ for the muttaṣil; يَا أَيُّهَا and قَالُوا إِنَّا for the munfaṣil.
Madd ʿāriḍ li-l-waqf: As for all readers, two, four or six ḥarakāt are allowed when stopping.

chapters.title: Two hamzahs in one word
paragraphs: General rule: The first, interrogative hamzah is always pronounced fully. Ibn Dhakwān pronounces the second fully too, with nothing between them, like Ḥafṣ, except in the special words below. Hishām's reading depends on the vowel of the second hamzah.

Second hamzah with fatḥah: Hishām has two ways, both with idkhāl (an alif inserted between the two hamzahs): tashīl of the second hamzah, or taḥqīq of it. Examples: ءَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ (2:6), ءَأَنتُمْ, ءَأَسْجُدُ (17:61).
Second hamzah with kasrah: Hishām reads both hamzahs with taḥqīq, with idkhāl or without it, as in أَئِذَا, أَئِنَّكُمْ and أَءِلَٰهٌ (27:60).

Seven places with idkhāl only: Hishām must insert the alif in أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ (7:81), أَئِنَّ لَنَا لَأَجْرًا (7:113 and 26:41), أَئِذَا مَا مِتُّ (19:66), أَئِنَّكَ لَمِنَ الْمُصَدِّقِينَ (37:52), أَئِفْكًا آلِهَةً (37:86) and أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَكْفُرُونَ (41:9). In the last one he has a further way: tashīl of the second hamzah with idkhāl.

Second hamzah with ḍammah: This occurs in three words. In أَؤُنَبِّئُكُم (3:15) Hishām reads taḥqīq with or without idkhāl. In أَءُنزِلَ (38:8) and أَءُلْقِيَ (54:25) he has those two ways and a third: tashīl of the second hamzah with idkhāl.

Added interrogative hamzah: Ibn ʿĀmir reads ءَأَذْهَبْتُمْ (46:20) with two hamzahs where Ḥafṣ has one; Hishām reads it with idkhāl and either tashīl or taḥqīq, and Ibn Dhakwān with taḥqīq of both. He also reads أَئِنَّكُمْ (7:81) and أَئِنَّ لَنَا (7:113) as questions where Ḥafṣ reads إِنَّكُمْ and إِنَّ لَنَا.
The word a-an kāna: In ءَأَن كَانَ ذَا مَالٍ (68:14) Ibn ʿĀmir reads two hamzahs (Ḥafṣ one) and the second is always read with tashīl: Hishām with idkhāl, Ibn Dhakwān without it.

Words with three hamzahs: In ءَامَنتُمْ (7:123, 20:71, 26:49), where Ḥafṣ has a single hamzah, and in ءَأَٰلِهَتُنَا (43:58), Ibn ʿĀmir reads the second hamzah with tashīl only. Idkhāl is not allowed, because the third hamzah has already become an alif.
The word aʿjamiyy: In أَعْجَمِيٌّ وَعَرَبِيٌّ (41:44) Hishām reads one hamzah only, as a statement. Ibn Dhakwān reads two hamzahs with tashīl of the second, like Ḥafṣ.
The word a-immah: أَئِمَّةَ is not a question. Hishām reads both hamzahs with taḥqīq, with idkhāl or without it.

chapters.title: The repeated question (istifhām mukarrar)
paragraphs: What it is: In eleven places a question comes twice in one passage, such as أَئِذَا ... أَئِنَّا.

General rule: Ibn ʿĀmir reads the first part as a statement with one hamzah and the second as a question: إِذَا كُنَّا تُرَابًا أَئِنَّا لَفِي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ (13:5). The same applies in 17:49, 17:98, 23:82, 32:10, 37:16, 37:53 and in al-ʿAnkabūt, إِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الْفَاحِشَةَ then أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الرِّجَالَ (29:28–29).

Three exceptions: In al-Naml the first is a question and the second a statement with an extra nūn: أَئِذَا كُنَّا تُرَابًا وَآبَاؤُنَا إِنَّنَا لَمُخْرَجُونَ (27:67). In al-Nāziʿāt likewise: أَئِنَّا لَمَرْدُودُونَ فِي الْحَافِرَةِ then إِذَا كُنَّا عِظَامًا نَخِرَةً (79:10–11). In al-Wāqiʿah (56:47) both parts are questions.
The two transmitters: Wherever the question is read, Ibn Dhakwān pronounces both hamzahs fully without idkhāl, and Hishām pronounces both fully with idkhāl only.

chapters.title: The single hamzah
paragraphs: Ibdāl: Ibn ʿĀmir turns the hamzah into a madd letter in يَاجُوجَ وَمَاجُوجَ (18:94, 21:96), مُوصَدَةٌ (90:20, 104:8) and سَالَ (70:1). Ḥafṣ reads يَأْجُوجَ وَمَأْجُوجَ, مُؤْصَدَةٌ and سَأَلَ.
Dropping the hamzah: He reads دَكًّا (18:98) for Ḥafṣ's دَكَّاءَ, and يُضَاهُونَ (9:30) for Ḥafṣ's يُضَاهِئُونَ.
The word minsaʾatahu: In 34:14 Ibn Dhakwān reads a sākin hamzah, مِنسَأْتَهُ. Hishām reads مِنسَأَتَهُ with fatḥah like Ḥafṣ.

Adding a hamzah: Ibn ʿĀmir reads مُرْجَئُونَ (9:106) and تُرْجِئُ (33:51) with a hamzah, هُزُؤًا and كُفُؤًا with a hamzah in place of Ḥafṣ's wāw, وَأَوْصَىٰ (2:132) for Ḥafṣ's وَوَصَّىٰ, and مِيكَائِيلَ (2:98) and زَكَرِيَّاءَ with a hamzah after the alif, which makes a madd muttaṣil.
The word al-bariyyah: In Sūrat al-Bayyinah Ibn Dhakwān alone reads الْبَرِيئَةِ with a hamzah. Hishām reads الْبَرِيَّةِ like Ḥafṣ.

chapters.title: Hishām's waqf on a word-final hamzah
paragraphs: Scope: When Hishām stops on a word that ends in a hamzah he lightens it (takhfīf); in waṣl he pronounces it fully. The lightening is either qiyāsī, by the rules of Arabic word forms (ibdāl, tashīl, naql, idghām), or rasmī, following the letter on which the hamzah is written in the muṣḥaf.

After a short vowel: The hamzah becomes the madd letter matching the vowel before it: alif after fatḥah (بَدَأَ is stopped on as بَدَا, اقْرَأْ as اقْرَا), yāʾ after kasrah (قُرِئَ, نَبِّئْ), wāw after ḍammah (اللُّؤْلُؤُ, امْرُؤٌ).
Hamzah with ḍammah or kasrah after a short vowel: Besides ibdāl there is a second qiyāsī way, tashīl with rawm, as in الْمَلَأُ, مِن نَّبَإِ, يَسْتَهْزِئُ and شَاطِئِ.

The rasmī way: Where the hamzah is written on a wāw or a yāʾ it is replaced by that letter, and the stop is made with sukūn, with rawm, or, for a ḍammah, with ishmām. Examples on wāw: يَبْدَؤُا, تَفْتَؤُا. Examples on yāʾ: يُبْدِئُ, and after an alif تِلْقَائِ and إِيتَائِ.

After an added wāw or yāʾ: When the wāw or yāʾ before the hamzah is not a root letter, the hamzah turns into the same letter and the two merge into one doubled letter: قُرُوءٍ becomes قُرُوٍّ, بَرِيءٌ becomes بَرِيٌّ and النَّسِيءُ becomes النَّسِيُّ. The stop is with sukūn or rawm, and also ishmām when the hamzah had ḍammah.

After an original wāw or yāʾ: Either naql, where the hamzah is dropped and its vowel moves to the wāw or yāʾ, which stays single, or idghām, where it is doubled. So شَيْءٍ is stopped on as شَيْ or شَيّ. The same applies to السَّوْءِ, سُوءَ, سِيءَ, جِيءَ, الْمُسِيءُ and لَتَنُوءُ.

After an alif: The hamzah becomes an alif, and the madd may be two, four or six ḥarakāt, as in جَاءَ and الدِّمَاءَ. If the hamzah had kasrah or ḍammah, two more ways are added, tashīl with rawm with four or with two ḥarakāt, giving five ways, as in السَّمَاءِ, يَشَاءُ and السُّفَهَاءُ.

chapters.title: Idghām and iẓhār
paragraphs: Dhāl of idh: Both transmitters merge it into dāl, as in إِذ دَّخَلُوا (15:52). Hishām also merges it into the other five letters, tāʾ, zāy, ṣād, sīn and jīm: إِذ تَّمْشِي (20:40), وَإِذ زَّيَّنَ (8:48), إِذ سَّمِعْتُمُوهُ (24:12). Ibn Dhakwān reads those five with iẓhār, like Ḥafṣ.

Dāl of qad: Both merge it into dhāl, ḍād, ẓāʾ and zāy: وَلَقَد ذَّرَأْنَا (7:179), فَقَد ضَّلَّ, فَقَد ظَّلَمَ. In وَلَقَدْ زَيَّنَّا (67:5) Ibn Dhakwān also has iẓhār. Hishām merges it into sīn, jīm, ṣād and shīn as well, as in قَد سَّمِعَ (58:1) and قَد شَّغَفَهَا (12:30), but reads لَقَدْ ظَلَمَكَ (38:24) with iẓhār. Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār in all of these.

Tāʾ al-taʾnīth: Ibn ʿĀmir merges it into thāʾ, ṣād and ẓāʾ: كَذَّبَت ثَّمُودُ, حَصِرَت صُّدُورُهُمْ (4:90), حُرِّمَت ظُّهُورُهَا (6:138). Hishām reads لَهُدِّمَتْ صَوَامِعُ (22:40) with iẓhār. Before sīn, jīm and zāy it is read with iẓhār.

Lām of hal and bal: Hishām merges it into tāʾ, thāʾ, ẓāʾ, zāy, sīn and ṭāʾ: هَل تَّرَىٰ (67:3), بَل طَّبَعَ (4:155), بَل زُّيِّنَ (13:33), هَل ثُّوِّبَ (83:36). He reads iẓhār before nūn and ḍād, and in أَمْ هَلْ تَسْتَوِي الظُّلُمَاتُ (13:16). Ibn Dhakwān reads iẓhār before all eight letters, like Ḥafṣ.
Dhāl into tāʾ: Ibn ʿĀmir merges the dhāl in اتَّخَذتُّمْ, أَخَذتُّمْ, لَاتَّخَذتَّ and similar forms. Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār.
Thāʾ into tāʾ: Ibn ʿĀmir merges the thāʾ in لَبِثتَّ and لَبِثتُّمْ. Hishām alone also merges it in أُورِثتُّمُوهَا (7:43, 43:72).
The words yalhath dhālika: In يَلْهَث ذَّٰلِكَ (7:176) Ibn Dhakwān reads idghām and Hishām iẓhār.

Other places: Ibn ʿĀmir merges the dāl of ṣād into the dhāl in كهيعص ذِكْرُ (19:1–2), the dāl into the thāʾ in يُرِد ثَّوَابَ (3:145), and the nūn into the wāw in يس وَالْقُرْآنِ (36:1–2) and ن وَالْقَلَمِ (68:1). Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār in all four.
No sakt: The four pauses of Ḥafṣ, at عِوَجًا (18:1), مَرْقَدِنَا (36:52), مَن رَّاقٍ (75:27) and بَل رَّانَ (83:14), are his alone. Ibn ʿĀmir joins without a pause.

chapters.title: Fatḥ and imālah
paragraphs: Meaning: Fatḥ is the plain open alif. Imālah here is the major imālah, the alif inclined halfway towards yāʾ.
Opening letters: Ibn ʿĀmir reads with imālah the rāʾ of الر and المر and the yāʾ of كهيعص (19:1).
Hishām's words: Hishām alone reads with imālah إِنَاهُ (33:53), مَشَارِبُ (36:73), آنِيَةٍ (88:5), and عَابِدُونَ and عَابِدٌ in Sūrat al-Kāfirūn (109:3–5).

Ibn Dhakwān, always with imālah: the ḥāʾ of حم in the seven surahs, the word التَّوْرَاة, the verbs جَاءَ and شَاءَ in their forms such as جَاءَهَا and جَاءَتْهُمْ, and الْمِحْرَابِ when it has kasrah (3:39, 19:11).
Ibn Dhakwān, the verb zāda: In فَزَادَهُمُ اللَّهُ مَرَضًا (2:10) he reads imālah only. Elsewhere he has both ways, with imālah preferred, as in فَزَادَتْهُمْ إِيمَانًا (9:124).

Ibn Dhakwān, the verb raʾā: Before a vowelled letter he reads imālah of the rāʾ and the hamzah, in waṣl and waqf: رَأَىٰ كَوْكَبًا (6:76), رَأَىٰ نَارًا. Before a sākin he reads fatḥ in waṣl and imālah only when stopping: رَأَى الْقَمَرَ, رَأَى الشَّمْسَ. With an attached pronoun he has imālah (preferred) and fatḥ: رَآهَا, رَآهُ, رَآكَ.

Ibn Dhakwān, two ways (imālah and fatḥ): هَارٍ (9:109), أَدْرَاكُم بِهِ (10:16) and وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ, الْمِحْرَابَ when it does not have kasrah, حِمَارِكَ (2:259), الْحِمَارِ (62:5), إِكْرَاهِهِنَّ (24:33), وَالْإِكْرَامِ (Sūrat al-Raḥmān) and عِمْرَانَ.

chapters.title: Waqf according to the script of the muṣḥaf
paragraphs: The word ayyuha: In three places written without an alif, أَيُّهَ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ (24:31), يَا أَيُّهَ السَّاحِرُ (43:49) and أَيُّهَ الثَّقَلَانِ (55:31), Ibn ʿĀmir reads the hāʾ with ḍammah in waṣl, أَيُّهُ, and stops on a sākin hāʾ, أَيُّهْ. Ḥafṣ reads fatḥah in waṣl.
The word yā abati: Ibn ʿĀmir reads يَا أَبَتَ with fatḥah on the tāʾ in waṣl and stops on it with a hāʾ, يَا أَبَهْ. Ḥafṣ reads يَا أَبَتِ and stops with tāʾ.

chapters.title: Yāʾāt al-iḍāfah
paragraphs: Meaning: The yāʾ al-iḍāfah is the first-person pronoun yāʾ, written in the muṣḥaf. The readers differ in 212 of them between fatḥah and sukūn. Only the places where Ibn ʿĀmir differs from Ḥafṣ are listed.

Before a hamzah with fatḥah: Ibn ʿĀmir reads fatḥah in لَعَلِّيَ: لَعَلِّيَ أَرْجِعُ (12:46), لَعَلِّيَ آتِيكُم (20:10, 28:29), لَعَلِّيَ أَعْمَلُ (23:100), لَعَلِّيَ أَطَّلِعُ (28:38), لَعَلِّيَ أَبْلُغُ (40:36). Hishām alone reads fatḥah in مَا لِيَ أَدْعُوكُمْ (40:41), and Ibn Dhakwān alone in أَرَهْطِيَ أَعَزُّ (11:92).

Before a hamzah with kasrah: Ibn ʿĀmir reads fatḥah in وَمَا تَوْفِيقِيَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ (11:88), آبَائِيَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ (12:38), وَحُزْنِيَ إِلَى اللَّهِ (12:86), وَرُسُلِيَ إِنَّ اللَّهَ (58:21) and دُعَائِيَ إِلَّا (71:6). He reads sukūn in يَدِي إِلَيْكَ (5:28), where Ḥafṣ has fatḥah.

Before the definite article: Ibn ʿĀmir reads fatḥah in عَهْدِيَ الظَّالِمِينَ (2:124), where Ḥafṣ has sukūn. He reads sukūn in آيَاتِي الَّذِينَ (7:146) and لِعِبَادِي الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا (14:31), where Ḥafṣ has fatḥah.
Before other letters, fatḥah: Ibn ʿĀmir reads fatḥah in وَأَنْ هَٰذَا صِرَاطِيَ مُسْتَقِيمًا (6:153) and أَرْضِيَ وَاسِعَةٌ (29:56).

Before other letters, sukūn: Ibn ʿĀmir reads a sākin yāʾ, kept in waṣl and waqf, in يَا عِبَادِي لَا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْكُمُ (43:68), where Ḥafṣ has no yāʾ. He reads sukūn where Ḥafṣ has fatḥah in وَلِي فِيهَا مَآرِبُ (20:18), وَمَا كَانَ لِي عَلَيْكُم (14:22), وَلِي نَعْجَةٌ (38:23), مَا كَانَ لِي مِنْ عِلْمٍ (38:69), and in the nine places of مَعِي that are not followed by a hamzah.
Where the transmitters differ: Hishām reads fatḥah like Ḥafṣ and Ibn Dhakwān reads sukūn in بَيْتِيَ (2:125, 22:26, 71:28), وَلِيَ دِينِ (109:6) and مَا لِيَ لَا أَرَى الْهُدْهُدَ (27:20).

chapters.title: Yāʾāt al-zawāʾid
paragraphs: Meaning: These are 62 word-final yāʾs that some readers pronounce although they are not written in the muṣḥaf.
Sūrat al-Naml: Ibn ʿĀmir reads فَمَا آتَانِ اللَّهُ (27:36) without the yāʾ in both waṣl and waqf. Ḥafṣ reads the yāʾ with fatḥah in waṣl.
Sūrat al-Aʿrāf: In ثُمَّ كِيدُونِ فَلَا تُنظِرُونِ (7:195) Hishām pronounces the yāʾ, كِيدُونِي, in waṣl and waqf. Ibn Dhakwān omits it like Ḥafṣ.

Sūrat al-Kahf: In فَلَا تَسْأَلَنِّي عَن شَيْءٍ (18:70), which Ibn ʿĀmir reads with fatḥah on the lām and a doubled nūn, Ibn Dhakwān has two ways in both waṣl and waqf: with the yāʾ, and without it, تَسْأَلَنِّ.

chapters.title: Notable individual words
paragraphs: Two sākin letters meeting: When a word-final sākin meets a verb beginning with hamzat al-waṣl whose third letter has a permanent ḍammah, Ibn ʿĀmir gives the first sākin a ḍammah: قُلُ ادْعُوا اللَّهَ أَوُ ادْعُوا الرَّحْمَٰنَ (17:110), أَوُ انقُصْ (73:3), فَمَنُ اضْطُرَّ, وَقَالَتُ اخْرُجْ (12:31), وَلَقَدُ اسْتُهْزِئَ. Ḥafṣ gives it a kasrah.

The same with tanwīn: When the first sākin is the nūn of a tanwīn, Hishām still gives it a ḍammah and Ibn Dhakwān gives it a kasrah, as in فَتِيلًا انظُرْ (4:49–50), مُتَشَابِهٍ انظُرُوا (6:99), مَحْظُورًا انظُرْ (17:20–21), مُنِيبٍ ادْخُلُوهَا (50:33–34). In بِرَحْمَةٍ ادْخُلُوا الْجَنَّةَ (7:49) and خَبِيثَةٍ اجْتُثَّتْ (14:26) Ibn Dhakwān has both ḍammah and kasrah.

Ibrāhām: Hishām reads إِبْرَاهَامَ, with an alif in place of the yāʾ, in 33 places: all of Sūrat al-Baqarah; the last three in al-Nisāʾ (4:125 twice, 4:163); the last in al-Anʿām (6:161); the last two in al-Tawbah (9:114); Ibrāhīm (14:35); al-Naḥl (16:120, 123); Maryam (19:41, 46, 58); the last in al-ʿAnkabūt (29:31); al-Shūrā (42:13); al-Dhāriyāt (51:24); al-Najm (53:37); al-Ḥadīd (57:26); and the first in al-Mumtaḥanah (60:4). Elsewhere he reads إِبْرَاهِيمَ. Ibn Dhakwān reads both ways in al-Baqarah only, and إِبْرَاهِيمَ in the rest of the Quran.

Ishmām: A little ḍammah is mixed into the kasrah of the first letter. Ibn ʿĀmir reads it in سِيءَ (11:77), سِيئَتْ (67:27), وَحِيلَ (34:54) and وَسِيقَ (39:71, 73). Hishām also reads it in وَغِيضَ (11:44), قِيلَ wherever it occurs, and وَجِيءَ (39:69, 89:23). Ḥafṣ reads a pure kasrah in all of them.

Other words listed: Ibn ʿĀmir also reads مُخْلِصًا (Ḥafṣ مُخْلَصًا), يَا بُنَيِّ (Ḥafṣ يَا بُنَيَّ), مُتُّ (Ḥafṣ مِتُّ), جُثِيًّا, عُتِيًّا and صُلِيًّا with ḍammah on the first letter, مِهَادًا in Sūrat Ṭā Hā (Ḥafṣ مَهْدًا), قُل رَّبِّي يَعْلَمُ and قُل رَّبِّ احْكُم in Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ (Ḥafṣ قَالَ), ثَمُودًا with tanwīn, الرُّعُبَ with ḍammah on the ʿayn, and بِيُوتًا with kasrah on the bāʾ.

doubts: The source has no section on the istiʿādhah, on mīm al-jamʿ, or on two hamzahs in two words, so no chapter was written for them.

Many verse numbers in the source are garbled or shifted by one or two (for example 46:19 for ءَأَذْهَبْتُمْ, 18:68 for فَلَا تَسْأَلَنِّي, 18:94 for دَكًّا, 19:74 for يَرْضَهُ, and several of the Ibrāhām places). References are given here in the standard Kufan numbering and should be verified.

Six hāʾ al-kināyah words (يُؤَدِّهِ, نُؤْتِهِ, نُوَلِّهِ, نُصْلِهِ, فَأَلْقِهِ, وَيَتَّقِهِ): the source says Hishām also reads them without ṣilah and marks one way as preferred, but it is not clear which; they are given simply as two ways. The source also calls Ibn ʿĀmir's reading of all six 'like Ḥafṣ', which does not hold for فَأَلْقِهْ and وَيَتَّقْهِ.
أَئِمَّةَ for Hishām: the source's note on which way (with or without idkhāl) is preferred is garbled, so no preference is stated.

The source lists 29:28 next to 7:81 as a place where Ibn ʿĀmir adds an interrogative hamzah, but its own list of repeated questions shows the first phrase of al-ʿAnkabūt as a statement; only 7:81 and 7:113 are stated as added questions.
The explanatory text of the repeated-question section has garbled ordinals; the rule was reconstructed from the source's own list of the eleven verses.
Opening letters with imālah: the source only says 'three cases' (الر, المر, كهيعص) without naming the letters; taken as the rāʾ and the yāʾ from the imālah marks in its text.

أَعْجَمِيٌّ (41:44): the primary source only says 'one hamzah'; that this is Hishām and that Ibn Dhakwān reads tashīl comes from the cross-check text. The iẓhār of tāʾ al-taʾnīth before sīn, jīm and zāy, and Ibn Dhakwān's iẓhār of lām hal/bal, are likewise confirmed from the cross-check text.
مَا لِيَ لَا أَرَى (27:20): the primary lists it among the sukūn words with a mark that seems to point to Ibn Dhakwān; Hishām's fatḥah is taken from the cross-check text.
كِيدُونِ (7:195): the source text says Hishām reads the yāʾ in waṣl and waqf, but its table seems to show a second way at waqf; only the first is stated.

The source's list of other individual words (page 29) is badly garbled and gives no verse numbers or per-transmitter detail; only the clearly identifiable words are included, and words that differ between the transmitters (such as وَرِءْيًا / وَرِيًّا and تَلَقَّفْ) were left out.
Pages 14–17 and 21–22 of the book (inside the chapter on Hishām's waqf on the hamzah) came out empty in the extracted text, so that chapter may lack detail that the book gives in tables.
